title: Playing a Shreveport veteran's funeral alone for ten dollars
summary: Love tells how he led a solo cornet funeral procession in Shreveport for a Spanish-American War veteran and joked with the pool-hall musicians afterward.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Oh yeah, you see, Shreveport, they never had no music for funerals around there at all, but they heard it by New Orleans. A lot of fellas coming down there and they'd see them funerals down there, you know, and some of them would remember. Well, they had a, he was a veteran from the Spanish-American War way back then. And it was his request to have some kind of music when you die, you know. So everybody knew I had been down this way, living down this way. They say, look, we got to have some kind of music at the funeral. I said, well, I'll tell you what you can do. I said, there ain't no brass band yet. We just make up the brass band and pay for them. What you charge for that? I said, oh, they used to charge about three or four dollars. I said, well, you'd have to pay about five dollars a piece. They said, no, I didn't want that many pieces, you know. I said, you don't know what the brass band is, do you? So they kept on saying, well, couldn't you kind of walk behind the hearse and play near Oh My God to thee or something like that, or some kind of church hand? Just use the cornet, just use. I said, you don't want no drum or nothing? I said, I can play any kind of way. They said, if you just want music. I said, yeah, I could play it. And say, when you get to the grave, play in the air, Oh My God to thee, say you use a veteran, say you go way out, buy the fence in the graveyard and make that last call there. I said, yeah, I can do that. I said, what'd that cost? I said, well, I mean, y'all, you ain't got no money. I said, I'll do it for ten dollars. So they paid me. Man, I come down to Texas Avenue, all the musicians, you know, they hang out around Jase's pool hall. They was all playing pool in there and they heard me blowing. What's that piece of, I said, near Oh My God to thee and they come out and seen the funeral. The fellas wanted me to wait, walk behind the hearse, you know what I said? I said, no, they don't do that the other way. Not in your honor. I said, let, they don't follow nobody to the graveyard. I said, let them follow you, you in front. Like the grand marshal said, you don't go behind the hearse that way. So I thought of that, you know, so I walked in front to her, leading the man to the grave. Brought him out there, you know, and got him out there. I played some kind of little hymn there. Then I went way out while he was bearing him in the corner of the yard, you know, way off. That's what it sounds sad though, you know, that I made that last call. And the fellow waved to me, you know, all over them. I'd make the call. And I'd come back to where they'd bury me back, you know, playing the air on my God as they'd let the preacher say a few words. And out we'd go. We didn't have to play going back, you know, just put my horn in the case. Had a little boy there tootin' my horn, I'd put you in the case. Went on up to the pool hall myself, you know. Then the fellow just laughed and said, man, what you doing in front of that hoist playing the air on my God to be? I said, man, how did he do that? Wouldn't you do it for ten bucks? And they all laughed then, you know. I said, come on, let's play some pool. I've got the pool again. I used to tell the fellas that I played a funeral by myself and they didn't believe me, you know. I said, go to Sweetport, they'll tell me. About when was that? That was way back. Let's see. That was about 1913. Just about. I might be missing it a year or two, but ain't many. 1913 or 14. That was about 20 bands playing. This one was playing, the next one playing. We was the last band, you know. We cut loose there with that piece that they played around. Oh, I can't think of it. We cut loose with that. They play what kind of pieces? They play at some special occasion or something? Or some neighborhood? No, Mardi Gras. They used to just all band, they call it the advertising band, you know. Chris Kelly, Rene A.
